title: Good Christian Men, Rejoice
description: John Mason Neale's carol to the old German tune In dulci jubilo, as he and Thomas Helmore printed it in 1854, for 2 to 4 singers: all three verses, each with its cry of "News! News!", "Joy! Joy!" or "Peace Peace!". A lively 6/8 in F, the alto moving in thirds and sixths under the tune.

credits.tune: "In dulci jubilo", an old German carol tune, as Thomas Helmore set it to Neale's words
credits.arrangement: Stackapella, on the chords of Bramley and Stainer's Christmas Carols New and Old

licence.words: public domain: John Mason Neale died 1866
licence.tune: public domain: an old German carol tune (Bramley and Stainer's index: "Old German"), as Thomas Helmore (died 1890) set it to Neale's words in Carols for Christmas-tide; Bramley and Stainer print the same tune
licence.arrangement: original, written for Stackapella: our own alto, tenor and bass under the tune as Neale and Helmore print it. The chords follow the four-part harmony of Bramley and Stainer's Christmas Carols New and Old, No. VIII, which is unsigned (the book's editors: John Stainer, died 1901, and Henry Ramsden Bramley, died 1917), so it was used only to check which chords are right, never copied part by part; Helmore's own four parts in the 1854 vocal parts, a different setting, are too small in the scan to read note by note and were not used. Our chords are theirs except: under the held "joice With" and "voice;" of each verse the lower parts hold a C chord (they keep F in the bass with F, B-flat and C chords over it), so the duet has E under the tune's C rather than their alto's octave; "heart," after it (and in verses 2 and 3) is B-flat over D (they keep F in the bass), so the bass doesn't meet the tune's fall from C to F in octaves; "Give" and "Ox" (and their places in verses 2 and 3) are A minor and the next quaver G minor 7 (they print F over A and B-flat), so the alto keeps E and F under the tune's C and D; the first "News!", "Joy!" and "Peace" are B-flat (they sing F in octaves); "Je-sus" and the second line's "He is" ("He hath", "gain His") are G minor 7 over D, as is the last "born" of each verse (they put B-flat in the bass); "born" in "born to-day:" and "man-" are D minor (they print F), and the quaver after each is C over E ("to-") or C7 over E ("ger") (they print B-flat over F under a passing G); "day:" (and "this!", "save!") is F with the alto on F and the tenor on C, so no part moves in octaves or fifths across the breath into "Ox"; the first "Christ is born to-" is B-flat over D, C and C7 (they print D minor over F, a passing chord and A7 over E), and the first "day!" holds an F chord under the tune's F and C (they move from D minor to C). One note a syllable in every lower part; the alto takes the chord's third wherever the tune hasn't it on every beat but those named below, so the duet and trio are complete harmony there; breaths written in for beginners ("voice;", "say:", "day:" and "now." and their places in verses 2 and 3 end a semiquaver early, verse 3's dotted "grave:" a dotted quaver early, so every part rests half a beat), and the last "save!" holds through the printed crotchet rest to the song's end. Accepted exceptions: the duet sings a bare fourth (F over C) on each verse's quaver pickup, on the quavers "ian" and "and" and the "And" before "He", and on "say:" ("bliss;", "grave:"), half a beat after its breath, where the alto can't reach A3 by step; the duet and trio go without the third on the quaver after each "Give"/"Ox" (a G minor 7 with D over G) and on "is" and "to-" in the last line, and the duet on the quavers C over E before "day:" and C7 over E before "now."; the alto sits more than an octave under the tune for the C of the first "day!", holding A3 under the tune's leap; the alto and tenor sing in unison (C4) on "ian men," and "and soul," so the tenor doesn't move in octaves with the tune; the soprano and bass leap into an octave (A to D, F to D) on the last line's first "Christ", accepted because it comes after the half-beat breath; verses 1 and 2 end on F without its fifth (tenor and bass on F3, leading into the next verse), and the song's last chord is complete, its tenor falling from E3 to C3 and its bass to F2, each at the bottom of its range for the held last note.
licence.source: The Condensed Vocal Parts to the Carols for Christmas-tide; set to Ancient Melodies by the Rev. T. Helmore, M.A.; the Words, principally in imitation of the original, by the Rev. J. M. Neale, M.A. (London: J. Alfred Novello, 1854), No. VI, "Good Christian men, rejoice.", pp. 20 and 21, marked Animato, in four parts on two staves in F major, 6/8, each of the three verses under its own music, written here in F in 6/8 as printed; the tune and all three verses as printed there, the long s modernised, "before him bow" and "Peace Peace!" as printed, and each verse's own rhythm kept (verses 1 and 2 sing the first "News!" and "Joy!" as a crotchet and a quaver rest, verse 3 the first "Peace" as a dotted crotchet); read from the scan at commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Condensed_Vocal_Parts_to_the_Carols_for_Christmas-tide.pdf (a Google scan of HathiTrust record 011630024), PDF pages 26 and 27 (index, PDF page 10). The chords checked against H. R. Bramley and John Stainer, Christmas Carols New and Old, first series (London: Novello, Ewer and Co.; this copy a printing of the 1870s, catalogued [187?]), No. VIII, "Good Christian men, rejoice.", pp. 16 and 17, in four parts in F major, 6/8, the same tune; University of California Libraries copy, archive.org/details/christmascarolsn00staiiala/page/n21 (music), n22 (verses 2 and 3) and n51 (index: words "The Rev. Dr. Neale", air "Old German"). Its words differ in small ways ("Good Christian men rejoice With heart and soul and voice,", "news! news!", "before Him bow", "Peace! Peace!", "Calls you one and calls you all,") and it sings each "News!" as a dotted crotchet; the first printing's are kept. The earliest known printing is the folio Carols for Christmas-tide, out by 28 October 1853, the date of the 1854 book's Notice, which refers to it (Wikimedia Commons PDF, p. 10)
